summary: Describes an ID extension to IMAP4rev1 that lets a client and server tell each other what program they are, to help in implementation identification.

eli5.summary: An email program and a server can say hello and exchange name tags, which helps in sorting out bugs.

questions: how to identify an imap client
what is the imap id command
is imap id a privacy risk
subtitle: An IMAP command that lets clients and servers tell each other what software they are, for bug reports and statistics.

tldr.problem: IMAP4rev1 gives no way to learn what client or server program is in use, which makes bug reports incomplete and usage statistics hard to gather.
tldr.mechanism: The ID command sends a list of field/value pairs such as name and version, and the server answers with its own list in an untagged ID response.
tldr.outcome: The information is for human consumption only: implementations MUST NOT change behavior, work around bugs or refuse service based on it.

today: RFC 2971 is a Proposed Standard from October 2000 and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why IMAP Needs an ID Command
sections.content:
IMAP4rev1 (RFC 2060) provides access to remote mail stores, but has no facility to advertise which program a client or server uses. That makes it hard for implementors to get complete bug reports, because it is often unclear which client or server is in use. Some sites also want usage statistics by client, which is difficult when users can get and maintain their own clients.

The ID command lets each side advertise information about its program, with contact information in case of bugs.
sections.eli5: When a mail program breaks, nobody knows which program was talking. The ID command lets each side say its name so the problem can be tracked.

sections.title: The ID Command and Response
sections.content:
A server advertises support by including the atom ID in its CAPABILITY list. The client then sends ID with a parameter list of field/value pairs, or NIL to send nothing but still accept a server answer. The command is valid in any state. A field may be any IMAP4 string, and a value may be any IMAP4 string or NIL, meaning the sender cannot or will not give it. The result is OK if the information is accepted, or BAD if the command is unknown or the arguments are invalid.

The server replies with an untagged ID response in the same format and a tagged result. A server MUST send a tagged response, but MAY send NIL in place of its list.
sections.eli5: The client says its name and details, and the server says its own back. Either side may say nothing if it prefers.

sections.title: Defined Fields and Limits
sections.content:
Any string may be a field, but the RFC defines these: name, version, os, os-version, vendor, support-url, address, date, command, arguments and environment. Implementations are free to send none, any or all of them, and strings are not case-sensitive.

Field strings MUST NOT be longer than 30 octets, value strings MUST NOT be longer than 1024 octets, and no more than 30 field-value pairs may be sent. The same field name MUST NOT be sent more than once. The RFC prefers finding the operating system name and version at runtime where possible.
sections.eli5: The name tag has standard boxes to fill in, such as program name, version and who made it, but there is a limit on how much you can write.

sections.title: Rules Against Acting on the Data
sections.content:
The sole purpose of the extension is statistical analysis and problem determination. Implementations MUST NOT make operational changes based on ID data. Servers MUST NOT work around client bugs, optimize for a particular client or deny service based on it, and clients MUST NOT do the same to servers.

The rationale is that ID must not replace the CAPABILITY mechanism with an ad-hoc approach where implementations guess each other's features from who they claim to be. Implementations MUST NOT send false information, and MUST NOT use contact information to submit automatic bug reports. They may include ID data in a prepared report, but must not send it without user authorization. They MAY send less information, or none, to protect privacy.

ID data is for human readers only. Never use it to decide how to behave.
sections.eli5: You may read the name tag, but you must not treat someone differently because of it. And you must not lie on your tag.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content: The grammar extends the IMAP4rev1 grammar. The ID command is added to command_any, and id_response is added to response_data. Both the command and the response carry an id_params_list, which is either a parenthesized list of string and nstring pairs or nil.
sections.eli5: This part spells out exactly how the message must be written so every program reads it the same way.

sections.title: Firewalls, Privacy and Security
sections.content:
Proxies and firewalls that alter an IMAP session must also change the ID command to advertise their presence. A firewall MAY block specific fields it thinks expose a vulnerability, but SHOULD NOT disable the extension entirely or unconditionally remove the client or server list. When handling a CAPABILITY response, a firewall MUST NOT let through extension names it does not know.

Privacy is the main danger. Clients and servers should tell users that ID is implemented and enabled, and it is highly desirable to allow disabling it, for example by sending NIL. Fields such as a processor ID number or Ethernet address can allow tracking of users. Knowing a program's version may also help an attacker exploit known holes.

Because ID needs no authentication and carries arbitrary data, a server that naively logs every ID command can have its log filled by an attacker. The RFC suggests truncating large responses, storing a single copy with a counter, keeping only interesting parts, and logging only for users who actually log in.
sections.eli5: Name tags can give away too much, like a home address, so people should be able to leave them blank. And a server should not write down every scribble that strangers hand it.
